t: How To Make A Warning Most Effective
q: In this way, it works like a consequence. It looks like a consequence. It acts like a consequence. It smells like a consequence. But in the truest sense, it isn’t a consequence. It’s a courtesy.
You see, other than being informed that they broke a class rule, nothing else happens to a student who first transgresses your rules.
Your only job is to inform, calmly and matter-of-factly— or even kindly and apologetically if the situation warrants—and then walk away without waiting for a response.
You no longer have to fret, sigh, harrumph, convince, coerce, question, glare, or otherwise make a show of your displeasure when a student misbehaves.
It becomes a simple courtesy you offer your students. An act of grace, trust, respect, and expectation that they will fix the problem.
x: Reframes the warning as a courtesy rather than a consequence.
A warning simply informs a student that a rule has been broken, with nothing further required of them, giving them a chance to self-correct before an actual consequence follows.
Argues warnings must be delivered calmly and matter-of-factly, then followed by walking away without waiting for a reaction.
Linsin reframes the classroom warning not as a consequence but as a courtesy, arguing that mislabeling it as a punishment undermines its purpose.
Reframes the warning as a courtesy rather than a consequence — informational only, requiring no action or response from the student.

t: How To Improve Behavior By Doing This One Thing
q: So I’ve broken down what students need to feel safe and ready to learn into three simple questions.
1. What’s next? 2. How long will it take? 3. Why are we doing it?
Whenever students are unsure or in the dark about any one or more of these, they begin to feel disconnected, as if education is being done to them rather than being an active participant.
It makes them feel that they’re important, respected, and tethered to the classroom.
Knowing how long eliminates anxiousness so they can listen and concentrate. And knowing why causes them to agree with and go along with your plans.
We free them to enjoy learning and being part of our classroom.
x: Frames answering these questions as making students feel respected, in control, and more willing to cooperate.
Linsin identifies communication as the often-missing ingredient for teachers who feel they're doing everything right yet still sense friction with their students.
Argues that leaving these questions unanswered causes students to feel disconnected, passive, frustrated, and less motivated.

q: I feel this pressure, too. Every year. And when I do feel it, I have learned to erase the list and create a new one.

With List 2, the never-finished nature is okay. Of course it's never finished, that list leads us to think, because something as deep and wide as the promotion of long-term human flourishing is always going on.
The meetings aren't the point, the clubs aren't the point, the tests aren't the point, the grades aren't the point. Much of the minutiae does have to get done.
A lot of time, the reason List 1 starts to drive me crazy is because I'm afraid of how I'll look if I don't get it done. What will the teacher down the hall think? What will my boss do?
My reputation is not the point. My ego's desire to be viewed as smart and competent and able to manage it all… not the point. Neither is my job security.

And what this does is it starts to actually make me better at doing List 1. I discern which of the items are just my ego, just my perfectionism. Which are furthest removed from promoting the long-term flourishing of my students?
x: Much of the pressure of the long list comes from fear of reputation and ego, which are not the purposes of school.
Replacing a sprawling to-do list with the single purpose of long-term student flourishing changes how the never-finished nature of teaching feels, from oppressive to expected.
Meetings, clubs, tests and grades are subordinate means, and are worth doing only insofar as they connect to student flourishing.
Both lists are never finished, but the first grinds teachers down toward countdown thinking, while the second makes unfinished work natural.
Dave Stuart Jr. follows his earlier post on the impossible list of things teachers feel expected to do by offering a way to reframe it.
Replacing a sprawling to-do list with the single purpose of long-term student flourishing changes how the never-finished nature of teaching feels, from oppressive to expected.

q: Obviously, this is a devastating list — devastating because it's familiar and real and authentic, and devastating because it sets us up for impossible frustration.

The mental picture I'm left with is of a drowning person, who in response to their drowning is thrown several bowling balls. It is no wonder that fewer people are drawn to education these days (below, a graph depicting the decline of teaching certificates in my state). Why would I want to enter a line of work that appears to suck the souls right out of teachers?

The good news is that even though teaching does suck the souls out of many who enter the field, it doesn't have to. Certainly, we've got some messed up policies in the USA, and we've got some detached bureaucrats ensuring compliance rather than solving problems, and there are states and systems that practically write, “We devalue teachers,” on giant billboards along the highway.

I'm sold out on the goodness of teaching, but I refuse to let it suck out my soul. I refuse to act under a list like the one at the start of this post. Why? Because it's an impossible list, and not every item on it is created equal.

And so that becomes a part of the work in systems where the pressure is insanely high. We set constraints, we force space for thinking, we start practicing the precious arts of satisficing and intentional neglect.

At the end of the day, we live where we live (unless we move) and we teach where we teach (unless we make a change). So, once we're here, no one is going to give us more time, and probably no one is going to come and tell us what we should stop doing so that the list is doable. In this case, it's simple and hard at the same time: we've just got to decide.
x: Stuart opens with a colleague's list of more than thirty things a secondary English teacher 'has to do' and calls it devastating precisely because it is familiar, authentic and impossible.
The post makes the teaching workload concrete with a long, relatable inventory of duties, which shows why good-faith teachers drown rather than blaming them for poor time management.
The closing line, 'we've just got to decide', locates the remedy in a teacher's own prioritisation rather than in waiting for relief from above.
Rather than blaming policy alone, he insists that teaching remains noble and that teachers must accept the list is not fixed and not every item on it is equal.
His move is to reframe the response to overload as a set of deliberate decisions: set constraints, force space for thinking, and practise satisficing and intentional neglect.
The piece ends by naming the decision as the real work, simple and hard at once, since no one is coming to tell teachers what to drop.

t: What It Really Means To Have High Expectations
q: It seems obvious, but the term has been repeated so often and for so long that its true meaning has been diluted.
They don’t come from a motivational poster . Your principal doesn’t bequeath them to you. And you darn sure won’t find them in a teacher’s guide.

They come from inside you. They’re developed over a lifetime of overcoming obstacles and disappointments. They’re born of perseverance, mental toughness, and the role models who passed them on to you.
This is why certain teachers can give a direction one time to a class they’ve just met and it’s followed. This is why some classes make unimaginable gains and unheard of test scores.
High expectations that come from within you, that relentlessly project their power upon your students, become part of them too. They imbue them with their own brand of gutsy, I’ll-show-them spirit.
x: Linsin argues that the phrase "high expectations" has become a cliche so overused that most teachers only vaguely grasp what it means.
That inner conviction, he writes, is not something a poster or a principal can hand a teacher.
He contends that high expectations are not techniques you deploy but a quality of character, born of a lifetime of overcoming obstacles, that must genuinely live inside the teacher.
This inner conviction explains why certain teachers can give one direction to a brand-new class and have it instantly followed.
A teacher's genuine high expectations become internalized by students, giving them their own resilient, determined spirit.

q: There is a mountain of misinformation about how to manage difficult students.
At best, it’s confusing, contradictory, and difficult to apply consistently.
Because, you see, most advice on how to deal with difficult students fails to address the root cause.
The entire notion that managing difficult students must be stressful, complicated, and a daily struggle is a myth in itself.
You realize that they’re just kids in need of direction and recalibration. They’re kids in need of someone to restore their dignity and switch on their intrinsic motivational engines.
Once you have an understanding of what they truly need it becomes not so difficult after all.
x: The belief that difficult students must be appeased, coddled, or bribed is itself identified as a harmful myth.
He argues the very premise that managing difficult students must be a stressful daily struggle is itself a myth.
The belief that difficult students must be appeased, coddled, or bribed is itself identified as a harmful myth.
